# Symbols Without Interior {#sec-ch-symbols-without-interior}

In 1948, Claude Shannon defined information as the reduction of uncertainty, measured in bits [@shannon1948mathematical]. But Shannon drew a deliberate boundary: "[t]hese semantic aspects of communication are irrelevant to the engineering problem." A bit is a unit of uncertainty, not of meaning. By conscious choice, he separated the syntactic from the semantic aspects of communication.

@sec-ch-properties-of-meaning listed what meaning looks like as geometry, and @sec-ch-curse-of-dimensionality showed why high-dimensional vectors have room for it and what the dangers and opportunities ahead are. Before building such vectors, this chapter asks why symbols alone cannot do the job. We start with what Shannon and Chomsky left out, symbols with no interior; we then see a table of one-hot symbols hit a geometric wall, and Rice's theorem put exact meaning out of reach even for programs. If exact meaning is out of reach, similarity must be graded, which is what @sec-ch-embedding-spaces builds.

## Shannon's Information Theory

Shannon measured the information of a message by its surprise. A message with probability $p$ carries $-\log_2 p$ bits of surprisal. Near-certain messages ($p \approx 1$) tell us almost nothing, while rare ones ($p \approx 0$) are highly informative. The *entropy* of a source is the average of this surprisal.

For a binary source that emits a one with probability $p$ and a zero with probability $1-p$, the average surprisal or entropy is:

$$
H_b(p) = -p \log_2 p - (1-p)\log_2(1-p),
$$

which peaks at one bit when $p = 1/2$ and vanishes when the outcome is certain (either $p = 0$ or $p = 1$). For a stream of $n$ bits that are independent and identically distributed, entropies add:

$$
H(X_1,\dots,X_n) = \sum_{i=1}^{n} H(X_i) = n\,H_b(p).
$$

Consider a faulty sensor that outputs a one with probability $p=0.99$ (see @tbl-binary-entropy). Seeing a one is unsurprising, while seeing a zero is a rare event. However, the average surprisal, or entropy, remains low. Even though zeros are highly informative individually, they occur so infrequently that the overall uncertainty of the source is small:

| $p$ | Surprisal of a one | Surprisal of a zero | Entropy $H_b(p)$ |
|:---:|:---:|:---:|:---:|
| 0.50 | 1.000 bits | 1.000 bits | 1.000 bits |
| 0.90 | 0.152 bits | 3.322 bits | 0.469 bits |
| 0.99 | 0.014 bits | 6.644 bits | 0.081 bits |

: Surprisal of each outcome and entropy of a binary source. {#tbl-binary-entropy}

Entropy is more than a measure of uncertainty. Shannon proved in the same foundational paper that it is also the limit of lossless compression. A source that emits independent symbols with entropy $H$ bits per symbol can be encoded, on average, in about $H$ bits per symbol, and no code can do better. For the faulty sensor with $p=0.99$, a complete log of 10,000 readings occupies 10,000 bits, but the entropy of the whole log is only $10{,}000 \times 0.081 \approx 810$ bits, which tells us that, in principle, we could reduce the storage by a factor of around 12. The savings come from giving frequent outcomes short codewords and rare ones long codewords, so that the length of each codeword approaches its surprisal. Long runs of ones become almost free, and the occasional zero pays for its surprise. Optimal coding techniques like Huffman and arithmetic coding, the engines inside every compressor, are practical ways of approaching this limit.

This gives entropy two readings that turn out to be the same: the average surprise of a source, and the minimum number of bits needed to describe it. This also connects compression with prediction. A good compressor is a good statistical model of its source, because the better we predict the next symbol, the shorter the code we can assign to it. We will see this identity again later in this chapter, when cross-entropy becomes the training loss function of neural networks.

Notice that the compressor needed to know the probabilities of the sensor, and nothing else. It never asked what a one represents, whether a temperature, a heartbeat or a coin flip. Shannon's theory is complete at that level, and the next section examines why that is both its strength and its boundary.


::: {.questions}
1. A sensor emits a one with probability $p = 0.8$ and a zero otherwise, independently at each step. Compute the surprisal of a one and of a zero, the entropy $H_b(0.8)$, and the minimum expected size, in bits, of a lossless encoding of a 10,000-symbol log. How does this compare with a fair coin?

2. A general sends one of two equally likely messages: "attack at dawn" or "attack at dusk". How many bits does each message carry according to Shannon? Now replace "attack at dusk" with the meaningless string "xqzv jwk", keeping its probability fixed. Does the entropy change, and what does this tell you about the relationship between entropy and meaning?
:::

::: {.answers}
1. The surprisal of a one is $-\log_2 0.8 \approx 0.32$ bits and that of a zero is $-\log_2 0.2 \approx 2.32$ bits. The entropy is their average, $H_b(0.8) = 0.8 \times 0.322 + 0.2 \times 2.322 \approx 0.72$ bits per symbol. By Shannon's source coding theorem, a 10,000-symbol log cannot be compressed losslessly below about $7{,}219$ bits on average, whereas a fair coin has $H_b(0.5) = 1$ bit per flip and needs the full 10,000 bits.

2. Each message has probability $1/2$, so it carries $-\log_2(1/2) = 1$ bit, and the source has an entropy of 1 bit. Replacing "attack at dusk" with "xqzv jwk" changes nothing. Entropy depends only on the probabilities of the messages, not on what they say. Relabelling the outcomes leaves it invariant, which is why Shannon could ignore meaning, and also why entropy alone can never tell us what a message means.
:::


## Shannon's Boundary Problem

Notice that the calculations above needed the probabilities of the symbols, and nothing else. The sensor could report temperatures, heartbeats or coin flips and its entropy would be the same. Ignoring meaning was not a weakness but the source of the theory's power. Because entropy depends only on probabilities, the same mathematics applies to any source and any channel, and it became foundational across computer science: the compression behind every ZIP, JPEG and MP3, the error-correcting codes in our disks, QR codes and mobile networks, the capacity limits that govern Wi-Fi and fibre, and, through cross-entropy, the loss function that trains modern neural networks. Shannon had already laid the other foundation of computing in his 1937 master's thesis, where he showed that Boolean algebra describes switching circuits [@shannon1937symbolic]. That algebra was George Boole's Laws of Thought of 1854, in which symbols that are true or false, with nothing in between, are combined by AND, OR and NOT to form any logical expression [@boole1854investigation]. But both foundations are discrete. A symbol is this one or that one, and a proposition is true or false.

However, that indifference to meaning is both the power of the theory and its boundary. The messages "attack at dawn" and "attack at dusk" can have the same probability, and therefore exactly the same information content, yet they mean very different things. A one-bit message has the same entropy whether it says that a coin landed heads or that it is raining today. For Shannon this was a feature, since the engineer's job is to deliver the message faithfully through a channel, not to understand it.

His collaborator Warren Weaver made the division explicit in 1949 [@weaver1949recent] by splitting the communication problem into three levels: **A**, the technical problem (how accurately can symbols be transmitted?); **B**, the semantic problem (how precisely do the symbols convey the desired meaning?); and **C**, the effectiveness problem (how well does the received meaning change behaviour?). Shannon solved level A. Embeddings are an attempt at level B, and the techniques that shape what a system does with the meaning it has received, such as alignment and tool use, are arguably attempts at level C. This book is mostly about level B. The three levels are a map of where embeddings sit. So far the symbols in this chapter have been words, but level B is not specific to text. Consider a blur of fur and a wagging tail in a photograph, a muffled bark heard through a closed door, or the uneven rhythm of paws on a staircase. To anyone who has met the animal, each of these conveys the same thing, and none of them is a word. Whether they can share one space with the word that names them, and with each other, is the test posed in the Prologue, to which we will return.

Shannon also showed, in the same 1948 paper, how far statistics alone can go. He generated English-like text by choosing each word according to how often it follows the previous one, and obtained [@shannon1948mathematical]:

> `THE HEAD AND IN FRONTAL ATTACK ON AN ENGLISH WRITER...`

Locally the text is plausible, since each word follows its predecessor with a believable frequency, yet globally it is meaningless. It is a language model in embryo, absorbing some of the syntax and none of the semantics. Some seventy years later, the same recipe with vastly more data and a far richer notion of context produced the large language models whose internal vectors we examine in @sec-ch-contextual-vectors. Shannon himself was wary of the hype that success brought. In "The Bandwagon" (1956) [@shannon1956bandwagon] he warned that information theory had become a fashion, and that borrowing its vocabulary for psychology, biology or linguistics did not make those fields more rigorous. Like relativity and quantum theory, it suffered the fate of successful scientific theories, as its words travelled much further than its mathematics. Yet the separation of form from meaning was not Shannon's alone. Linguistics reached it independently.

::: {.questions}
1. Take a plain-text book from the Internet (for example, from Project Gutenberg) and compute the probability of each letter. What is the entropy of this distribution, and how does it compare with $\log_2 26$?

2. With the same book, compute the probability of each word. What is its entropy? Where does the difference with the letter entropy come from?

3. Finally, estimate the probability of each word given the previous $n$ words and use it to generate a random phrase. How does the result change as $n$ grows from 1 to 3?
:::

::: {.answers}
3. Download a book as plain text, lowercase it, count the letters `a`–`z` with `collections.Counter`, and apply $H = -\sum_i p_i \log_2 p_i$ to the relative frequencies:

   ```python
   import re
   from collections import Counter
   from math import log2

   def entropy(counts):
       n = sum(counts.values())
       return -sum(c / n * log2(c / n) for c in counts.values())

   text = open("book.txt", encoding="utf-8").read().lower()
   print(entropy(Counter(re.findall(r"[a-z]", text))))
   ```

   The complete, self-checking script is `shannon_letter_entropy.py`. For English prose the result is about $4.1$ to $4.2$ bits per letter (4.18 for *Pride and Prejudice*), below the maximum $\log_2 26 \approx 4.70$ of a uniform alphabet because letters are very unevenly used (`e`, `t`, `a` are frequent, `z`, `q`, `j` rare). Strip the Project Gutenberg header and licence first if you want a clean estimate.

4. Reuse `entropy` on the words, `Counter(re.findall(r"[a-z']+", text))` (script `shannon_word_entropy.py`). A novel gives roughly $9$ to $11$ bits per word (9.11 for *Pride and Prejudice*, with about 7,000 distinct words), far above the letter entropy. The reason is the size of the alphabet. A word is drawn from thousands of possibilities, not from 26, so each symbol carries more surprise. The fair comparison is per character. Dividing by the average word length plus the space (about 5.4 characters) gives roughly $1.7$ bits per character, much lower than $4.2$. Words capture the spelling constraints between letters, which the single-letter model ignores. Shannon's 1951 estimates, which let humans guess the next letter, reached a similar order of magnitude of about one bit per letter [@shannon1951prediction]. Note that the plug-in estimate underestimates the entropy for short texts, as rare words are under-sampled.

5. Build a table that maps each context of $n$ consecutive words to the list of words that followed it in the book, then repeatedly sample the next word from the list of the current context (sampling from a list with repetitions reproduces the empirical probabilities):

   ```python
   import random
   from collections import defaultdict

   words = re.findall(r"[a-z']+", text)
   n = 1                                   # context length; n = 1 is Shannon's word-pair model
   model = defaultdict(list)
   for i in range(len(words) - n):
       model[tuple(words[i:i + n])].append(words[i + n])

   out = list(random.choice(list(model)))
   for _ in range(40):
       out.append(random.choice(model.get(tuple(out[-n:]), words)))
   print(" ".join(out))
   ```

   The script `shannon_ngram_text.py` runs this for $n = 1, 2, 3$ and measures how much of the output is copied from the book. With $n = 1$ the output resembles Shannon's sample. Each pair of neighbours is plausible, but the sentence wanders and means nothing. With $n = 2$ and $n = 3$ it becomes more fluent, and from $n = 3$ on it starts copying long passages verbatim from the book. In a single book most contexts of three words occur only once, so the model has no choice but to repeat the source. Larger contexts need exponentially more data and memory, the trade-off that neural models of natural languages solve by compressing the context into a dense vector, an embedding [@bengio2003neural].
:::

## Chomsky's Staircase: Structure Without Meaning

The same separation between the form of a message and what it means appeared in linguistics within a decade of Shannon's paper. Chomsky classified formal languages by the grammars that generate them [@chomsky1956three], and each step of his staircase was later shown to match a machine that recognizes exactly the languages those grammars generate, each machine adding a different kind of memory. A finite automaton has no memory beyond its current state, so it recognizes the regular languages, whose patterns depend only on a bounded amount of recent history. A pushdown automaton adds a stack, a last-in first-out memory of unbounded size, which is exactly what is needed to match nested structure such as balanced parentheses (push when a bracket opens, pop when it closes), recognizing context-free languages. Linear-bounded automata, which recognize the context-sensitive languages, get a working tape as long as the input, and Turing machines, at the top, get an unbounded tape.

The staircase classifies sets of strings, a string being either accepted or rejected, but the same machines can also make random choices, with a probability attached to each possible move. On the bottom step this gives the probabilistic finite automaton, of which the $n$-gram model, the Markov chain and the hidden Markov model are familiar examples, and which can both generate strings and score how likely a given string is. On the context-free step it gives the probabilistic context-free grammar, whose rewriting rules carry probabilities, together with its machine, the probabilistic pushdown automaton. At the top, it gives a Turing machine whose actions include drawing random numbers, which is what any program that calls a random number generator is. Across the different steps, the probabilities decide which strings are likely, not what the machine can remember and therefore recognize, so the memory of each step stays the same.

Shannon's word-pair text comes from a bigram model, the probabilistic version of the bottom step, in which the previous word alone sets the probabilities of the next word. Its only memory is that previous word, so it cannot even remember whether it has opened a parenthesis. Surprisingly, a programming language can touch two steps at once, because it has two different aspects, and each sits on a different step. Consider this Python program:

```python
n = int(input())
while n != 1:
    n = n // 2 if n % 2 == 0 else 3 * n + 1
```

Its syntax, meaning whether the text is a well-formed program, is a question for the parser. The parser must check, for instance, that brackets and blocks are properly nested, which needs the stack of a pushdown automaton, so it sits one step above the bottom. The grammar is written in Backus–Naur form, and parsing is decidable and fast. The parser always finishes, and it never needs to run the program. Its runtime behaviour, meaning what happens when the program runs, can also be turned into a question about sets of strings, for example the set of all programs that eventually stop. This is a language just like the set of well-formed programs, and we can ask which machine recognizes it. A parser is not enough, because whether a program stops is not visible in its text.

For example, does the loop above, which iterates the Collatz map, stop for every positive starting number? Nobody knows, and reading the program text does not tell. The only general way is to run the program and wait. A Turing machine can do exactly that, by simulating the program step by step, and it answers yes if the program stops. If the program never stops, the machine runs forever and never answers no. No weaker machine recognizes this language, because simulating an arbitrary program requires an unbounded memory and arbitrary computation. General-purpose languages are Turing complete, so this aspect sits at the very top. The same program text therefore belongs to two languages: the set of well-formed programs, which is close to context-free, and the set of programs that stop, which only a Turing machine can recognize.

Yet each step of the Chomsky hierarchy adds structure, not meaning. A parser can tell you that `x = y + 1` is well formed, but not what `x` is for. What a program *means* is what it does, and Rice's theorem, which we will meet two sections ahead, says that this cannot in general be read off its text.

A programming language has a precisely formalized grammar but no meaning in its symbols. Natural language has the opposite profile, a rich meaning but a grammar that resists formalization. Both worlds share one design decision, which is that the symbol itself is atomic, an identity with no interior. `dawn` and `dusk` are as different to a parser as `dawn` and `xqzv`. Programmers know this well. Swapping one name for another in a single place can change what a program does (`print(x)` and `send(x)` call different functions), but renaming consistently, in its definition and in every use, leaves the behaviour unchanged (a property known as alpha-equivalence), and so does renaming `print` to `show` throughout the language and its libraries. The same holds, at least in principle, for a natural language. In a universe where everybody exchanged the words `send` and `receive` in every sentence ever spoken, no meaning would be lost, because the link between the form of a word and its meaning is arbitrary. In both worlds, then, the meaning is not in the shape of the symbol but in its relations to the other symbols, and what differs is where those relations are recorded. In a program they are written down explicitly, as definitions of functions and types, and the machine only ever checks names for equality and follows those definitions. Whatever else a human reads in `customer_balance` was smuggled in by the author. In natural language nobody wrote the definitions down. "Attack at dawn" is not "attack at dusk", and the reason is not an entry in a table but what speakers know about dawn and dusk, when they happen and how they relate to each other and to an attack. These relations, spread over the use of a word, are the interior that the symbol itself lacks, its meaning.

Linguistics offered only coarse ways out. A tag such as `NOUN` is the coarsest description of a word that could be built by hand, a class label that says almost nothing about it, although it is the first hint that a symbol can be given an interior. Parse trees are tree-shaped, a hint that hierarchies will need a geometry of their own (@sec-hyperbolic-spaces). Since a symbol has no interior to read such structure from, we must look instead at its relations with other symbols. `dawn` keeps different company from `dusk`. It appears near `sunrise`, `morning` and `early`, while `dusk` appears near `sunset`, `evening` and `late`. So a word can be known by the company it keeps. Words that keep similar company tend to have similar meanings, an idea that linguists call the *distributional hypothesis*, and the company of a word is something we can count in a large body of text. Counting is what statistics does well.

Anyone who has searched a database with ``WHERE content LIKE '%monarch%'`` and found no trace of "king" or "queen" has met the limit of matching symbols. The database only compares them for equality, and `monarch` is not equal to `king`, however close their meanings are. Equality is the whole geometry of a symbol table, and the next section shows how poor that geometry is. Written as one-hot vectors, every pair of distinct symbols sits at exactly the same distance, $\sqrt{2}$, so `dawn` is no closer to `dusk` than to `xqzv`. Giving symbols an interior, so that distance carries meaning, is what the rest of this chapter is about.

::: {.questions}
1. Write a program that decides whether a string of brackets `()[]{}` is balanced, using a stack.

2. Write a program that decides whether a string belongs to $\{a^n b^n c^n : n \ge 0\}$ (e.g., "aabbcc" belongs to the set, but "aaabbbcc" does not) using no memory other than the input itself: a tape as long as the input, which you may overwrite, and a constant number of variables. Then try to adapt your stack-based solution of the previous question. What goes wrong?

3. Write an interpreter for MiniBrainf***, a tiny Turing-complete language. Its machine is a tape of cells, all starting at 0 and extending without limit to the right, with a head on the first cell. A program is a string of seven instructions, executed in order: `>` and `<` move the head one cell right or left; `+` and `-` add or subtract 1 from the current cell; `.` prints the current cell; `[` jumps forward to the matching `]` if the current cell is 0; `]` jumps back to the matching `[` if the current cell is not 0. Run `++++++++[>++++++++<-]>+.`, then run `+[>+]` and `+[]` with a limit on the number of steps. Why can no linear-bounded automaton do what your interpreter does?
:::

::: {.answers}
6. Push every opening bracket onto a stack. On a closing bracket, pop and check that the popped bracket is its partner. Accept if no check failed and the stack is empty at the end:

   ```python
   PAIRS = {")": "(", "]": "[", "}": "{"}

   def balanced(s):
       stack = []
       for ch in s:
           if ch in PAIRS.values():
               stack.append(ch)
           elif ch in PAIRS:
               if not stack or stack.pop() != PAIRS[ch]:
                   return False
       return not stack
   ```

   The script `chomsky_balanced_brackets.py` runs it on a few balanced and unbalanced examples. With a single kind of bracket a counter would be enough, but with several kinds the machine must remember which bracket is open, in order, which is why `([)]` is rejected.

7. Cross off one `a`, one `b` and one `c` per pass, overwriting the cells in place, and accept when all three letters run out together:

   ```python
   def in_language(s):
       if not re.fullmatch(r"a*b*c*", s):  # a finite automaton checks the shape
           return False
       tape = list(s)
       while True:
           crossed = 0  # how many of a, b, c we crossed off in this pass
           for symbol in "abc":
               head = 0
               while head < len(tape) and tape[head] != symbol:  # scan right
                   head += 1
               if head < len(tape):
                   tape[head] = symbol.upper()  # cross it off
                   crossed += 1
           if crossed == 0:
               return True  # all three letters ran out together
           if crossed < 3:
               return False  # one letter ran out before the others
   ```

   The script `chomsky_anbncn.py` checks it against the definition on every string of up to nine letters. The program never leaves the input. It overwrites cells and keeps a constant number of variables, which is exactly what a linear-bounded automaton may do. The stack-based solution fails because the stack is consumed. Pushing the `a`'s and popping one per `b` matches the first two counts, but when the `b`'s are done the stack is empty and nothing is left to compare the `c`'s with. The adapted program accepts $a^n b^n c^m$ for every $m$, for example `aabbccccc`, so it recognizes the context-free language $\{a^n b^n c^*\}$ and not the context-sensitive one. That no pushdown automaton can do better is proved by the pumping lemma for context-free languages.

8. The interpreter needs a program counter, a tape that grows on demand, and a table of matching brackets:

   ```python
   from collections import defaultdict

   def run(program, max_steps=100_000):
       jump, stack = {}, []
       for i, op in enumerate(program):  # match the brackets once, with a stack
           if op == "[":
               stack.append(i)
           elif op == "]":
               j = stack.pop()
               jump[i], jump[j] = j, i

       tape, ptr, pc, out, steps = defaultdict(int), 0, 0, [], 0
       while pc < len(program) and steps < max_steps:
           steps += 1
           op = program[pc]
           if op == ">": ptr += 1
           elif op == "<": ptr -= 1
           elif op == "+": tape[ptr] += 1
           elif op == "-": tape[ptr] -= 1
           elif op == ".": out.append(tape[ptr])
           elif op == "[" and tape[ptr] == 0: pc = jump[pc]
           elif op == "]" and tape[ptr] != 0: pc = jump[pc]
           pc += 1
       return out, len(tape), pc >= len(program)  # printed values, cells used, halted?
   ```

   The script `chomsky_bf_interpreter.py` runs the three programs. The first prints `[65]`, since $8 \times 8 + 1 = 65$. The second, `+[>+]`, never halts and touches a new cell at every iteration. After 10,000 steps it has used 3,334 cells, and the number grows with the time allowed. The third, `+[]`, loops in place forever. With the step limit we can only give up, never conclude that they will not stop. A linear-bounded automaton cannot do this for two reasons. First, its tape is as long as its input, whereas `+[>+]`, a five-character program, needs a tape that keeps growing. Second, it has only finitely many configurations (tape contents, head position and state), so running it long enough either halts or repeats a configuration, and its halting is decidable. For Brainf*** programs the halting problem is undecidable, which is the Turing machine's extra power, and the same halting problem is behind Rice's theorem, two sections ahead.
:::

## The Orthogonal Catastrophe: Why Symbolic Tables Hit a Geometric Wall

Shannon's theory and Chomsky's staircase are both purely symbolic, and both leave meaning out. Entropy, as we saw, depends only on probabilities, so Shannon's theory is unchanged if every symbol is relabelled. Chomsky's staircase measures how much memory a machine needs to decide whether a string belongs to a language, from a bare state to a stack, a bounded tape and an unbounded tape, but all four steps take the same alphabet for granted. A finite automaton decides what to do next by looking up its current state and the symbol it just read in a transition table. A pushdown automaton pushes and pops symbols and checks whether the top one is the one it expects. A Turing machine reads and writes symbols on its tape. In every case the only question a machine can ask about two symbols is whether they are the same. The staircase measures how much *structure* a machine can keep track of, not how much *meaning* its symbols carry, because as far as the machine is concerned they carry none. Both theories, then, are built on symbols that share nothing with one another, no feature and no direction through which meaning could pass from one to the next. Written as vectors, every such symbol sits at a right angle to every other and equally far from all of them, and we will call this the **orthogonal catastrophe**.

To see the catastrophe in action we need to write symbols as numbers, since computers can only process numbers. The standard way to do this is **one-hot encoding**. We fix an ordering of the vocabulary $\mathcal{V}$, a list of $|\mathcal{V}|$ distinct symbols, and represent the $j$-th symbol by a vector with $|\mathcal{V}|$ entries, all equal to 0 except for a single 1 in position $j$ (the "hot" entry). Take a toy vocabulary of five words:

| Word | Vector | $i=1$ | $i=2$ | $i=3$ | $i=4$ | $i=5$ |
|:---|:---|:---:|:---:|:---:|:---:|:---:|
| `dawn` | $\mathbf{e}_1$ | 1 | 0 | 0 | 0 | 0 |
| `dusk` | $\mathbf{e}_2$ | 0 | 1 | 0 | 0 | 0 |
| `king` | $\mathbf{e}_3$ | 0 | 0 | 1 | 0 | 0 |
| `queen` | $\mathbf{e}_4$ | 0 | 0 | 0 | 1 | 0 |
| `xqzv` | $\mathbf{e}_5$ | 0 | 0 | 0 | 0 | 1 |

: One-hot encoding of a five-word vocabulary. Each row is the vector $\mathbf{e}_j \in \mathbb{R}^5$ of a word, and the column $i$ gives its $i$-th entry, $(\mathbf{e}_j)_i = 1$ if $i = j$ and $0$ otherwise. {#tbl-one-hot}

A one-hot vector is just the position of a word in the vocabulary, written as a vector instead of as a number, so the word is its index and the index is the word, like the line number of an entry in a dictionary. It is also how the bottom step of the staircase looks in linear algebra. If the state of a finite automaton is written as a one-hot vector, reading a symbol is multiplying it by a matrix of zeros and ones that moves the single 1 to the next state. A probabilistic automaton uses a matrix of transition probabilities instead, and Shannon's bigram model is the same idea. Its table has one row per word, holding the probabilities of every word that can follow it, and multiplying the one-hot vector of the previous word by the table selects that word's row. In all these cases the one-hot vector acts as a pointer into a transition table, a matrix.

Multiplying by a matrix is one thing we can do with a one-hot vector; the other is to compare it with a second vector. The natural way to turn a pair of vectors into a single number is the **dot product**, $\langle \mathbf{u}, \mathbf{v} \rangle = \sum_k u_k v_k$, which multiplies the two vectors entry by entry and adds the results. Each position in which both vectors are large contributes to the sum, so the dot product measures how much they have in common. Two vectors with dot product zero are **orthogonal**, which geometrically means that they form a right angle. For vectors with non-negative entries, such as one-hot vectors, orthogonality means that no position is active in both, so informally they share nothing. For one-hot vectors, the dot product with $\mathbf{e}_i$ selects the $i$-th entry of the other vector, $\langle \mathbf{e}_i, \mathbf{v} \rangle = v_i$, and when $\mathbf{v} = \mathbf{e}_j$ that entry is 1 only if the two words are the same, so the dot product is a test for equality,

$$
\langle \mathbf{e}_i, \mathbf{e}_j \rangle = \delta_{ij} =
\begin{cases} 1 & \text{if } i = j, \\ 0 & \text{if } i \neq j, \end{cases}
$$

where $\delta_{ij}$ is the Kronecker delta. Distances follow immediately. Expanding the squared norm of the difference and using $\|\mathbf{e}_i\| = 1$,

$$
\|\mathbf{e}_i - \mathbf{e}_j\|_2^2 = \|\mathbf{e}_i\|^2 + \|\mathbf{e}_j\|^2 - 2\langle \mathbf{e}_i, \mathbf{e}_j \rangle = 1 + 1 - 0 = 2,
$$

so $\|\mathbf{e}_i - \mathbf{e}_j\|_2 = \sqrt{2} \approx 1.414$ for *every* pair of distinct words. In the toy vocabulary we defined earlier, `dawn` is exactly as far from `dusk` as from `xqzv`, and `king` is as far from `queen` as from `dawn`. The **cosine similarity** of two vectors is their dot product divided by the product of their lengths, $\cos\theta = \langle \mathbf{u}, \mathbf{v} \rangle / (\|\mathbf{u}\| \, \|\mathbf{v}\|)$, the cosine of the angle $\theta$ between them: 1 if they point in the same direction, 0 if they are orthogonal, and $-1$ if they point in opposite directions. One-hot vectors have length 1, so their cosine similarity is just their dot product, 0 for every pair of distinct words. Whether we measure the distance between two words or their cosine similarity, the answer to "how similar are these two words?" is the same for all pairs, $\sqrt{2}$ in one case and 0 in the other, and therefore uninformative.

One-hot vectors are equidistant, and equidistance is more than an inconvenience. It is the geometry of maximal ignorance, and it has four consequences, two of which the questions at the end of this section probe. The first is that there is no such thing as "nearby". The nearest neighbours of `king` are all the other $|\mathcal{V}|-1$ words, always at distance $\sqrt{2}$, so retrieval, clustering and similarity search have nothing to work with. This is the `LIKE '%monarch%'` wall of the previous section in geometric form.

The second consequence is that what is learned about one word does not transfer to similar words. A linear model reading a one-hot vector computes $\langle \mathbf{w}, \mathbf{e}_i \rangle = w_i$, one independent parameter per word, so learning that "attack at dawn" is a military order tells it nothing about "attack at dusk", and a word that rarely appears gets a parameter that is barely trained.

The third is that the geometry is blind to renaming. Permuting the coordinates, which is the same as relabelling the words, preserves every distance. This is the vector form of the alpha-equivalence we met for programs, where renaming `customer_balance` to `x7` changes nothing, and it is harmless as long as the renaming is applied everywhere, to the representation and to the use of the words alike. The defect is that the one-hot geometry is the same for every assignment of words to coordinates. It holds no information about how any word relates to any other, so nothing in it can tell a correct assignment from a scrambled one. Give `dawn` the vector of `king` while the words keep their use, and a one-hot representation cannot notice. A representation that holds meaning must.

Finally, the dimension grows with the vocabulary. A space of dimension $D$ contains at most $D$ mutually orthogonal non-zero vectors, so $|\mathcal{V}|$ words forced to be orthogonal need $|\mathcal{V}|$ dimensions. With a vocabulary of 50,000 words, each vector has 49,999 zeros and a single 1, and every new word adds a dimension to the space.

The flaw lies in the encoding itself. The distances between one-hot vectors are fixed before any data is seen, and a model that reads one-hot vectors can only learn one independent parameter per word, so more examples of `dawn` never tell it anything about `dusk`. If similarity is to exist, it must be built into the representation itself. Each word needs a position in a space whose geometry is not the trivial one, so that `dawn` can lie close to `dusk` and far from `xqzv`. The way out is surprisingly simple. We multiply the one-hot vector $\mathbf{e}_i$ by a matrix $\mathbf{E} \in \mathbb{R}^{|\mathcal{V}| \times d}$ with $d \ll |\mathcal{V}|$, mapping the $|\mathcal{V}|$-dimensional vectors to $d$-dimensional ones. Since $\mathbf{e}_i$ has a single 1 in position $i$, the product $\mathbf{e}_i^\top \mathbf{E}$ is just the $i$-th row of $\mathbf{E}$, a dense vector of $d$ real numbers. If the rows are learned instead of fixed, they are free to move closer together or farther apart. Such a matrix is an **embedding**, and the rest of this chapter and of the book will revolve around how embeddings work and where their values come from.

But why do we need geometry at all to represent meaning? We could keep the symbols as they are and decide, once and for all, which of them mean the same thing, grouping `king` with `monarch` in a table of synonyms instead of placing them close together. A thesaurus of this kind can be built, but it is costly to write and it only says same or different. The next section asks how far exact sameness of meaning can go in the best case, for a programming language, where meaning is a precise mathematical object, and even then finds a hard limit. That limit is what motivates a graded notion of similarity, which is what an embedding provides.

::: {.questions}
1. A finite automaton accepts the binary strings with an even number of 1s. Write its state as a one-hot vector of length 2 (even, odd) and give a $2 \times 2$ matrix to each input symbol, so that reading a symbol is a matrix–vector product. Check the result against the parity of the 1s on all strings of up to 10 symbols. What do the columns of these matrices look like, and how would they change for a probabilistic automaton?

2. Consider a logistic regression without bias, $p = \sigma(\langle \mathbf{w}, \mathbf{x} \rangle)$ with $\sigma(t) = 1/(1+e^{-t})$, trained on examples $(\mathbf{x}, y)$ with $y \in \{0, 1\}$ to minimize the cross-entropy loss $L = -y \ln p - (1-y)\ln(1-p)$, where $p$ is the probability that the model assigns to the label 1 for the input $\mathbf{x}$ and $L$ is the surprisal of the observed label $y$ under the model (the box *How a model learns: gradient descent* below explains how the loss is minimized, and Learning by Prediction returns to the cross-entropy). Derive the gradient $\nabla_{\mathbf{w}} L$ and write the gradient descent update of $\mathbf{w}$ with learning rate $\eta$. Which weights change when $\mathbf{x}$ is a one-hot vector? Then train the model to label `dawn` as 1 ("is a time of day") and `king` and `queen` as 0, twice: with one-hot inputs, and with the hand-made dense vectors of the table below, whose values are illustrative and not learned (`xqzv` gets a small noise vector). What probability does each model assign to `dusk`, which it never saw during training, and to `xqzv`?

   |:---|:---:|:---:|:---:|:---:|:---:|

   | `king` | 0 | 1 | 1 | 0.5 | 0 |
   | `queen` | 0 | 1 | 1 | $-0.5$ | 0 |
   | `xqzv` | 0.2 | $-0.3$ | 0.1 | 0.3 | $-0.1$ |

Then exchange the labels `dawn` and `king` in the dense table of the previous question, so that each word receives the other's vector, and compare the distance between `dawn` and `dusk` before and after. What does the difference tell you about which of the two representations can contain meaning?

::: {.answers}
9. Let $\mathbf{s} = (1, 0)$ be the initial state "even" and let reading a `0` multiply by the identity and reading a `1` by the matrix that swaps the two states:

    ```python
    import itertools
    import numpy as np

    T = {"0": np.array([[1, 0], [0, 1]]), "1": np.array([[0, 1], [1, 0]])}

    def accepts(s):
        state = np.array([1, 0])        # one-hot vector of the initial state "even"
        for ch in s:
            state = T[ch] @ state       # reading a symbol = multiplying by its matrix
        return bool(state[0])           # accept if the final state is "even"

    for n in range(11):                 # every binary string of up to 10 symbols
        for bits in itertools.product("01", repeat=n):
            s = "".join(bits)
            assert accepts(s) == (s.count("1") % 2 == 0)
    ```

    The script `onehot_dfa.py` verifies `accepts(s) == (s.count("1") % 2 == 0)` on all strings of up to 10 symbols. In a deterministic automaton every column of every matrix has exactly one 1 and the rest zeros (a permutation matrix here, in general a 0/1 matrix), because each state moves to exactly one next state. In a probabilistic automaton each column holds the probabilities of the next state, so the entries are in $[0, 1]$ and every column sums to 1 (a column-stochastic matrix). For example, if a `1` flips the state with probability $0.9$, the matrix is $0.9\,T_1 + 0.1\,T_0$, and after reading `111` the state is $(0.244, 0.756)$. The one-hot vector is the special case of a state with all its probability on one entry.

10. The derivation is the example in the callout "How a model learns: gradient descent": $\nabla_{\mathbf{w}} L = (p - y)\,\mathbf{x}$, and the update is $\mathbf{w} \leftarrow \mathbf{w} - \eta\,(p - y)\,\mathbf{x}$. If $\mathbf{x} = \mathbf{e}_i$ is one-hot, only $w_i$ changes, $w_i \leftarrow w_i - \eta\,(p - y)$, and every other weight stays where it was. Training on one word cannot alter what the model says about any other. The update is a single line of code, and the script `onehot_transfer.py` also checks the gradient against finite differences:

    ```python
    import numpy as np

    WORDS = ["dawn", "dusk", "king", "queen", "xqzv"]
    ONE_HOT = np.eye(5)
    DENSE = np.array([[1, 0, 0, 0, 0.4],        # dawn
                      [1, 0, 0, 0, -0.4],       # dusk
                      [0, 1, 1, 0.5, 0],        # king
                      [0, 1, 1, -0.5, 0],       # queen
                      [0.2, -0.3, 0.1, 0.3, -0.1]])  # xqzv: noise
    y = {"dawn": 1.0, "king": 0.0, "queen": 0.0}  # the only labelled words

    def sigmoid(t):
        return 1 / (1 + np.exp(-t))

    def train(x, steps=500, lr=0.5):
        w = np.zeros(x.shape[1])
        for _ in range(steps):
            for word, label in y.items():
                xi = x[WORDS.index(word)]
                w -= lr * (sigmoid(w @ xi) - label) * xi  # w <- w - lr * (p - y) * x
        return w

    for x in (ONE_HOT, DENSE):
        print(sigmoid(x @ train(x)).round(3))  # probability for each of the five words
    ```

    For `dawn`, `dusk`, `king`, `queen` and `xqzv` the script gives the probabilities $(0.996, \mathbf{0.5}, 0.004, 0.004, \mathbf{0.5})$ with one-hot inputs and $(0.997, \mathbf{0.984}, 0.001, 0.001, \mathbf{0.812})$ with dense inputs, after 500 passes with a learning rate of 0.5. The exact values depend on these choices. Without a bias the training data are separable, so the weights keep growing and the probabilities keep moving towards 0 or 1 the longer we train, but the pattern of the answers does not change. With one-hot vectors the weights $w_{\text{dusk}}$ and $w_{\text{xqzv}}$ never move from 0, since no training example has a 1 in those coordinates, so the model has learned nothing about them and answers $\sigma(0) = 0.5$ for both. With dense vectors the model learns a positive weight on "time of day" and negative ones on "person" and "royal", and `dusk` inherits the answer because it shares the first feature with `dawn`. This is transfer: what is learned about one word moves to the words that are close to it. The price is that the same mechanism acts on `xqzv`, which means nothing. Its noise vector projects onto the learned weights and the model answers $0.812$, an arbitrary value with no more meaning than the noise. Transfer is only as good as the vectors, which is why the rest of the chapter is about where they come from.

11. Relabelling the words permutes the rows of the matrix of vectors, and the distances between the new rows are those of the old ones with their labels permuted. The script `onehot_renaming.py` loops over `itertools.permutations(range(5))` and confirms that `distances(E[list(perm)])` equals `distances(E)` for all 120 of them. This holds in general. A permutation of the coordinates of $\mathbb{R}^{|\mathcal{V}|}$ is an isometry, and permuting the words of a one-hot basis is the same as permuting the coordinates. In the dense table, exchanging `dawn` and `king` changes the distance between `dawn` and `dusk` from $0.80$ to $1.85$, because `dawn` now has the vector of a king. The one-hot geometry cannot tell a correct assignment of words from a scrambled one, so it contains no information about which word is which except for identity. It is the geometry of alpha-equivalence, in which `customer_balance` and `x7` are interchangeable. A representation that can contain meaning must be sensitive to this exchange, since the words keep their use while their vectors are swapped, and `dawn` still appears with `breaks`, not with `wears`.
:::

::: {.callout-note title="How a model learns: gradient descent"}
A model has **parameters**, here the weights $\mathbf{w}$ and later the rows of an embedding matrix, and a **loss** $L$, a number that is small when the model fits the data and large when it does not. Training, or model fitting, is the search for parameters with a low loss. Gradient descent is one method for finding such parameters, and it does so by following the slope of the loss function. The **gradient** $\nabla_{\mathbf{w}} L$ lists how much the loss changes when each parameter is nudged, and it points in the direction in which the loss grows fastest, so a small step in the opposite direction lowers the loss:

$$
\mathbf{w} \leftarrow \mathbf{w} - \eta\,\nabla_{\mathbf{w}} L.
$$

The **learning rate** $\eta > 0$ sets the size of the step: too large and the steps overshoot the valley, too small and they crawl. Training repeats the step until the loss stops decreasing.

As an example, take the logistic regression of the second question, with one training example $(\mathbf{x}, y)$. Since $\sigma'(t) = \sigma(t)(1-\sigma(t))$, we have $\partial p / \partial \mathbf{w} = p(1-p)\,\mathbf{x}$ and, by the chain rule,

$$
\nabla_{\mathbf{w}} L = \left(-\frac{y}{p} + \frac{1-y}{1-p}\right) p(1-p)\,\mathbf{x} = (p - y)\,\mathbf{x}.
$$

Gradient descent therefore updates $\mathbf{w} \leftarrow \mathbf{w} - \eta\,(p - y)\,\mathbf{x}$: the weights move by a multiple of the input, in the direction that reduces the error $p - y$. If the model says $p = 0.9$ for an example with $y = 0$, the error is $0.9$ and $\mathbf{w}$ moves against $\mathbf{x}$, which lowers $\langle \mathbf{w}, \mathbf{x} \rangle$ and so $p$. If it already says $p \approx y$, the step is almost zero.

When the loss is a sum with one term per example, so is its gradient, and computing it means going through all the data. **Stochastic gradient descent** (SGD) instead takes the term of one example, or of a small batch, picked at random. Each step is cheap and noisy, but on average it points in the same direction as the full gradient, so many small steps end up in the same place.

What can be promised depends on the shape of the loss. A convex loss, such as that of a logistic regression, has no false valleys. Wherever it stops decreasing, it is at its lowest point, so small enough steps head towards it. (When the data are perfectly separable, as in the exercise, the loss has no lowest point. It tends to 0 without ever reaching it, and the weights grow without bound, so the loss converges but the weights do not.) The losses of embeddings and neural networks are not convex. Gradient descent finds a low point, not necessarily the lowest, and different starting points can end at different parameters.
:::

## Rice's Theorem: Why Exact Meaning Is Out of Reach

Perhaps human language is too complex and nuanced, and meaning is easier to extract from formal languages. Could we simplify the problem by extracting meaning from the symbols of our beloved programming languages? For words, the equidistance of one-hot symbols is unacceptable, but programs have an advantage, since their meaning is not vague. The meaning of a program is a mathematical object, a (partial) function that maps each input to the output of the program, or to nothing if it never halts. Then symbols might be rescued from their equidistance without any geometry. All we would need is a procedure that takes two programs and decides whether they give the same output on every input. Programs could then be sorted into classes of equal meaning. Consider bubble sort and insertion sort. Their texts differ, so as symbols they are as far apart as `dawn` and `xqzv`, yet they compute the same function and any user would call them the same program. This is equality of *meaning*, of what a program does rather than how it is written, and it is exactly what Shannon left out by design and what Chomsky's staircase does not measure. If it is possible to extract meaning from symbols anywhere, it is in the world of programming. Rice's theorem says that it cannot be done.

Rice's theorem [@rice1953classes], which generalizes Turing's proof that the halting problem is undecidable [@turing1936computable], says that every interesting question about what a program does, as opposed to what it looks like, is undecidable. A question is about what a program does when its answer depends only on the function the program implements, its meaning, and it is interesting when some programs pass it and others fail it. Rice's insight is that undecidability is not specific to the halting problem---whether a program stops or loops forever---but extends to every question about the behaviour of programs.

It is fascinating how many of the familiar limitations in software engineering are this theorem in disguise. No static analyser can promise to find every null-pointer dereference without raising false alarms, because "does this program ever dereference null?" is a question about behaviour. No antivirus can flag every malicious program without also flagging some harmless ones, because "does this program do harm?" is also a question about behaviour. Scanning the text for known patterns only moves the problem, since the author of the malware can rewrite the text and keep its behaviour unchanged. Tests can refute a program but never prove it correct, because a failing test is a counterexample anyone can check, while a thousand passing ones leave open the thousand-and-first input. And a compiler will never, on its own, turn bubble sort into insertion sort, let alone into merge sort. It cannot decide whether two programs are equivalent, so it applies a small library of rewrites, each known to be safe in advance.

It would be a mistake to read the theorem as "nothing can be known about programs". It forbids a single procedure that is general, always terminating and exact, all at the same time. Give up generality by restricting the questions or the programs, give up termination by accepting a procedure that may never answer, or give up exactness by settling for approximate answers, and the impossible becomes possible.

Giving up generality opens four doors, two that restrict the questions and two that restrict the programs, but each leads away from what we were looking for, a procedure that groups programs by meaning. The first door is questions about the text of a program rather than its behaviour. Whether a program contains a `while` loop or has balanced brackets is settled by a parser, but the text is exactly what bubble sort and insertion sort do not share, so grouping by text keeps them as far apart as one-hot symbols. Syntax, the subject of Chomsky's staircase, is untouched by the theorem, and so is its blindness to meaning. The second door is questions with a time limit. Whether a program halts and prints 65 has no general answer, because if it is still running after an hour, we cannot tell whether it is about to stop or will loop forever. But if we ask instead whether it halts and prints 65 *within one second*, we run it for one second and stop it: either it has already printed 65 and halted, or it has not, and in both cases we have our answer. The limit turns an endless wait into a finite one, but the question is no longer about meaning alone. The meaning of a program is the function it computes, which says which output comes out of each input but not how long it takes to come out. Bubble sort and insertion sort compute the same function, yet on the same list one may finish within the second and the other not, so a question with a time limit can separate two programs that mean the same thing. Its answer depends on how a program computes, not only on what it computes. The third door is weaker machines, those that are not Turing complete. Whether two regular expressions accept the same strings is decidable, while the same question for two context-free grammars is not, so meaning can be decided only for machines too weak to write most programs, and the staircase turns out to be a trade-off between expressiveness and the questions we are still allowed to ask. Finally, the fourth door is to focus on particular programs. Bubble sort and insertion sort can be proved equivalent by hand, and verified compilers carry a machine-checked proof that each of their rewrites preserves meaning for every program, but grouping programs by meaning would require automating the proof for all programs, which is exactly what no one can do.

Giving up termination leaves a procedure that may never answer, which gives one-sided evidence. Running a program will eventually confirm "halts and prints 65" if it holds, but for a program still running we can never get a firm "no".

So exact meaning cannot be read from the text of a program, and after giving up generality and termination, what remains is to give up exactness. Whatever notion of similar meaning we use for code has to be approximate and graded, a distance rather than an identity, and that is what an embedding provides. In the previous section each word received a dense vector, and the distance between two vectors said how similar the words were. We can do the same for programs, filling in the vector from what a program does rather than from how it is written. Choose a fixed set of inputs, say thirty short lists, run each program on them, and use the outputs, one after another, as the successive coordinates of its vector. The distance between two programs is then how much their outputs differ on these inputs. Call this a *behavioural embedding*. Bubble sort and insertion sort give the same outputs, so they land on the same point, while a program that sorts in descending order lands elsewhere. A positive distance proves that two programs differ, since some input tells them apart, but a zero distance proves nothing, since two programs can agree on every chosen input and differ on one that was never tried. This is the one-sided evidence of the previous paragraph, turned into geometry.

In the behavioural embedding we decide what each coordinate means, the output on each input we chose, and the computer only fills in the values. An embedding can also be learned, its coordinates fitted to data rather than designed, and it can be learned from the text alone. In 2019, code2vec [@alon2019code2vec] was an early learned code embedding, placing snippets with similar purpose close together. It learned from their syntax, the text that the first door showed to be blind to meaning, and still it found similar purposes, because code written for the same purpose tends to be written in similar ways. A single text says nothing certain about what its program does, but the regularities across many texts say a great deal. Like the behavioural embedding, code2vec does not escape Rice's theorem, but it gives up even the one-sided guarantee that a positive distance proves two programs differ, since a distance between two snippets proves nothing about what they do. It trades the impossible exact answer for a useful graded one. Learned code embeddings have since been developed much further, and the section on learning by contrast will show how such embeddings are trained.

We turned to programs because they looked like the easy case, a formal language whose meaning is precise, a function from inputs to outputs, and even there no procedure can retrieve that meaning exactly from the text. Words are even harder. Their meaning is not a function, nor anything else we know how to write down exactly, so for words there is not even an exact answer for a procedure to fail to compute. If exact meaning is out of reach where it is well defined, there is little hope of reaching it where it is not. Words also lack what gave us the behavioural embedding, since there is no input on which to run a word and no behaviour to observe. What is left is what code2vec used, the regularities in how symbols are used across many texts. For words, the regularity is the company a word keeps, and the next chapter, @sec-ch-embedding-spaces, starts by counting it.

::: {.questions}
1. Take this program, which counts how many steps the Collatz iteration needs to reach 1:

   ```python
   def steps(n):
       count = 0
       while n != 1:
           n = n // 2 if n % 2 == 0 else 3 * n + 1
           count += 1
       return count
   ```

   Ask an LLM what it does and what `steps(27)` returns, then run it to check. Write down which model you used and the date. Then keep varying the program and keep asking: rename the variables, replace the loop by recursion, add dead code, change `3 * n + 1` into `3 * n - 1`, and finally ask whether a program that tries the even numbers 4, 6, 8, ... and stops at the first one that is not the sum of two primes ever halts. How do you know when an answer is right? For each answer that is wrong or unsure, classify the failure: a limit of this model, which a better one might overcome, or a limit of the problem, which no model could overcome. Whatever your model answered, which variations fall in each class? If you found an LLM that always described correctly what a program does, would it disprove Rice's theorem?

2. In this exercise a program is a Python generator, which does one step of work each time it reaches a `yield` and returns its result when it ends.

   ```python
   def quick():
       yield
       return 65

   def slow():
       for _ in range(5000):
           yield
       return 65

   def forever():
       while True:
           yield
   ```

   Write `check(program, budget)`, which runs a program for at most `budget` steps and returns `True` if it ends with the result 65, `False` if it ends with another result, and `None` ("unknown") if the budget runs out first. Try it on the three programs and on one of your own that returns 1, with budgets of 10 and 10,000. For which program does a larger budget change the answer? For the `forever` generator, does `check` ever stop answering `None`, however large the budget? Why can it not simply answer `False` after a very large number of steps?

Compare two ways of representing five programs: `bubble_sort`, `insertion_sort`, `sort_descending`, `identity` and `sort_unless_huge`, which sorts any list with fewer than 1,000 items and returns longer ones unchanged. In the first, each program is a symbol, a one-hot vector. In the second, it is the vector of its outputs on 30 random lists of 6 digits, concatenated. Compute the matrix of Euclidean distances for both representations. What does each say about `bubble_sort` and `insertion_sort`, and about `bubble_sort` and `sort_unless_huge`? Find an input that proves two of the programs different, and explain why a distance of zero between two programs proves nothing while a positive distance proves something. How does this connect to Rice's theorem?

12. The script `rice_llm_probe.py` gives the ground truth for the variations. `steps(27)` returns 111, and so do the recursive version and the version with other names, dead code and a different control structure. A correct description is the same for all three, because they are the same behaviour in three texts. Changing `3 * n + 1` into `3 * n - 1` changes the behaviour with one character. The sequence from 27 now falls into a cycle and never reaches 1. Tracing a few steps reveals it, and a hasty description keeps describing the original. This failure is a limit of the model, since tracing settles it. Note that here the answer can be certain, because the program has no state other than `n`, so a repeated value proves that it loops forever. The last program is different. It halts if and only if Goldbach's conjecture is false, and nobody knows whether it is, although no counterexample has been found among the numbers checked, up to $4 \times 10^{18}$ as of 2014. An LLM can say that it probably never halts because the conjecture is believed true, and that is a bet and not an answer. If it answers "it halts" or "it does not halt" with confidence, nothing in the answer lets us check it. This failure is a limit of the problem. No model, however good, can settle it.

    A good LLM does not disprove Rice's theorem, for three reasons. First, the theorem is about one fixed procedure that is correct on *every* program and always gives an answer, and a conversation tests the LLM on the programs a person thinks of, which are short, readable and mostly benign. "It was right every time we asked" is a statement about a sample. Second, an LLM is itself a program with a finite set of weights that produces its answer in finitely many steps. If it were right about every program, it would be the decider the theorem forbids. Third, we could not tell. To certify the LLM we need the correct answer for each question, and for the programs that matter, such as the Goldbach one, nobody has it. What a good LLM does is behave like a step-limited tester, with a far richer notion of "step". It answers correctly on the programs whose behaviour can be read off, and for the others it either says that it cannot tell or, worse, it is confidently wrong. In evaluations of 2026, its error rate tends to grow with the length and complexity of the programs [@sultan2026llms] and is generally somewhat higher when a program or its input is perturbed [@spiess2026how], which is the graded, approximate kind of answer that Rice's theorem leaves open and that this chapter is about.

13. Call `next` on the generator once per step, and stop when the generator ends or the budget runs out:

    ```python
    def check(program, budget):
        steps = program()
        for _ in range(budget):
            try:
                next(steps)
            except StopIteration as done:
                return done.value == 65      # the program ended: a firm True or False
        return None                          # the budget ran out: unknown
    ```

    The script `rice_semidecider.py` runs the tests. `quick` gives `True` with both budgets, and a program that returns 1 gives a firm `False`. `slow` gives `None` with a budget of 10 and `True` with a budget of 10,000, since it needs 5,001 calls to `next` to end. `forever` gives `None` with every budget, and no budget can do better. After a million steps the tester cannot tell `forever` from a program that would end at step a million and one, so it can never answer `False`. A larger budget can turn `None` into `True` or `False`, but only for programs that end. A firm `False` for every program would need a procedure that decides, for every program, whether it ends with the result 65, and since this is a question about what the program does, Rice's theorem says that no such procedure exists. What survives is one-sided: if the program ends with 65, waiting long enough will confirm it.

14. The script `rice_behavioural_embedding.py` builds both representations. As symbols, the five programs are the rows of the identity matrix and every pair is at distance $\sqrt{2} \approx 1.41$. `bubble_sort` is as far from `insertion_sort` as from `identity`, the orthogonal catastrophe in a new vocabulary. As behaviour vectors of 180 numbers (30 lists of 6 digits), the distances are:

    | | bubble | insertion | descending | identity | unless_huge |
    |:---|:---:|:---:|:---:|:---:|:---:|
    | bubble | 0 | 0 | 71.6 | 50.1 | 0 |
    | insertion | 0 | 0 | 71.6 | 50.1 | 0 |
    | descending | 71.6 | 71.6 | 0 | 53.6 | 71.6 |
    | identity | 50.1 | 50.1 | 53.6 | 0 | 50.1 |
    | unless_huge | 0 | 0 | 71.6 | 50.1 | 0 |

    The distance is graded: `bubble_sort` and `insertion_sort` coincide, `identity` is nearer to the sorters than `sort_descending` is, and the groups have a structure that one-hot vectors could not express. But `bubble_sort` and `sort_unless_huge` are also at distance 0, although they are different functions. They disagree only on lists of 1,000 items or more, such as `list(range(1000, 0, -1))`, which none of the probes comes close to. A positive distance is a proof: any probe on which the two outputs differ, for example any list that is not already sorted for `bubble_sort` and `identity`, is a counterexample to equality that can be checked. A zero distance is only the absence of evidence, since finitely many probes cannot cover the infinitely many inputs. This is Rice's theorem seen from the side of embeddings: deciding whether two programs are the same function is impossible, but we can find differences by testing and obtain a graded similarity from the tests that survive, with no guarantee for the rest. Learned code embeddings do the same with a far richer notion of behaviour.
:::

## Symbols With No Inside

This chapter has gone from Shannon to Rice and from one-hot vectors to the impossibility of representing meaning, showing that meaning cannot reside in the symbols themselves. Shannon's definition of information does not include the meaning of the message at all, and Chomsky's staircase adds memory according to the grammatical structure without giving the symbols an interior. A table that gives each word its own one-hot vector puts every pair of words at the same distance, so no pair is nearer than any other. And Rice's theorem shows that the obstacle is not only the vagueness of words, since even for programs, whose meaning is a precise function, no procedure can group them by meaning exactly.

The above considerations show that meaning cannot reside in the symbols themselves. Nearness has to be a matter of degree (@sec-prop-nearness), and difference has to be something the geometry can express (@sec-prop-difference). In this chapter, a formal definition of meaning seems to be out of reach, and what remains is the intuition that a graded distance for words could convey meaning. Perhaps studying how symbols co-occur across many texts will reveal patterns that one-hot vectors cannot capture, and the next chapter, @sec-ch-embedding-spaces, starts by counting those co-occurrences.
